title: 基于循环神经网络的自适应几何优化算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm for geometric optimization, leveraging the power of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to dynamically adjust optimization parameters based on the input data's evolution. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with complex data and lack adaptability, while current approaches frequently rely on static parameters. This work introduces a system where an RNN learns a representation of the geometric shape and adapts the optimization process based on the data's trajectory. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through the application of the algorithm to a diverse set of optimization problems, achieving significant improvements in convergence speed and solution quality compared to existing methods. The core mechanism involves the RNN's learning of feature representations, which are then used to influence the optimization process, enabling the algorithm to navigate complex geometric landscapes more effectively. This results in a robust and adaptable optimization strategy.

title: Probability Arithmetic: A Novel Approach to Numerical Computation
abstract: This paper introduces Probability Arithmetic, a novel computational paradigm that integrates probability logic with arithmetic operations. We propose a new mechanism for calculating high-dimensional probability models by combining the "probability update" mechanism of probability logic with the "addition" and "multiplication" of arithmetic operations. The core of this approach lies in dynamically updating probabilities based on a combination of these operations, enabling efficient and scalable computations for complex probability scenarios. This system aims to significantly enhance numerical capabilities, particularly in the context of large-scale probability modeling, offering a potentially transformative advancement in data analysis and machine learning.

title: Quantum Topology for Nonlinear Equation Solving
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to solving complex mathematical problems, particularly within the realms of quantum mechanics and topological physics, utilizing quantum topology. We propose a new method for constructing and applying non-linear equation-solving algorithms based on the inherent properties of quantum topology. The core mechanism centers around leveraging the self-adaptive nature of quantum states to effectively navigate and resolve intricate mathematical challenges. This approach offers the potential for significantly enhanced computational speed and efficiency compared to traditional methods, offering a promising avenue for advancing research in these fields. The paper details the development of a specific quantum algorithm and discusses its potential impact on solving problems such as the Schrödinger equation and the study of topological phases of matter.

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Encoding (QIE)
abstract: Quantum Entanglement Information Encoding (QIE) explores the utilization of quantum entanglement as a fundamental building block for enhanced data transmission and processing, specifically targeting advancements in quantum key distribution (QKD) and quantum computing security. This research proposes a novel encoding scheme predicated on the unique properties of entangled states, aiming to overcome limitations of traditional methods. The core mechanism centers around leveraging entanglement to ensure secure and efficient data transfer and manipulation, offering a fundamentally new approach to information handling within the quantum realm. The study investigates the potential of QIE to significantly improve the reliability and security of quantum communication protocols, particularly in safeguarding cryptographic keys and bolstering the robustness of quantum computations. This paper presents a detailed examination of the proposed encoding strategy, its potential benefits, and preliminary results demonstrating its feasibility and effectiveness within the context of quantum information processing.

title: 拓扑学与量子计算的融合模型
abstract: This paper investigates the potential for a unified model integrating topology and quantum computation, specifically focusing on the analysis of quantum systems and their associated topological structures. We propose a novel framework that combines established topological concepts with quantum mechanical principles to provide a deeper understanding of these intricate phenomena. The core aim is to identify novel applications of quantum computation within the realm of topological physics, exploring how quantum algorithms can be leveraged to uncover and manipulate topological properties. This research aims to advance our understanding of the relationship between topology and quantum mechanics, potentially leading to new theoretical insights and practical applications. The work will examine various aspects of this integration, including the representation of topological phases, quantum algorithms for topological data analysis, and the potential for topological quantum error correction. The paper will conclude by discussing the challenges and future directions of this research.

title: Node-Level Mechanism-Shift Detection in Linear Non-Gaussian Causal Networks: A Bootstrap-Based Framework with Application to the Human Gut Microbiome
abstract: As microbiome research increasingly seeks to identify true ecological shifts, transitioning from associational to causal approaches is essential. However, detecting structural changes across independent networks remains challenging due to the absence of established biological ground truths and the small, imbalanced sample sizes typical of microbiome cohorts. To address this, we extend an existing network comparison framework to enable node-level mechanism-shift detection under the direct linear non-Gaussian acyclic model (DirectLiNGAM). We evaluate the Naive, Bootstrap, and Relative sample size Bootstrap Stability (RSBS) estimators across extensive synthetic discovery runs and a semi-synthetic, batch-corrected human gut microbiome cohort. Our results demonstrate that resampling-based estimation consistently outperforms a single-fit Naive baseline by trading marginal recall for substantial precision gains. On both semi-synthetic and synthetic data, standard Bootstrap is optimal for comparing datasets of equal size, whereas RSBS is the only estimator that reliably handles imbalanced cohorts. This advantage strengthens as network dimensionality increases and persists under authentic compositional noise. Navigating this complex and emerging research area is currently constrained by limitations in data quantity and quality, scarce biological knowledge, and a lack of dedicated software. To address these critical gaps, we provide the complete benchmark pipeline and synthetic data generators as an open-access Python package, causal-comparator, to support node-level mechanism-shift detection across systems biology applications.

title: MEOX: Compact Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts for Earth Observation
abstract: Recent advances in Earth Observation representation learning accommodate heterogeneous sensors and missing observations, often through larger architectures. We present MEOX (Multimodal Earth Observation with eXperts), a multimodal masked autoencoder with a 2.939 million-parameter encoder and 3.115 million parameters in total. Sensor-specific adapters, explicit validity signals, and a shared sparse-expert block preserve modality-dependent processing before a learned patch-wise fusion. Four metadata tokens then accompany a single spatial sequence through fourteen further encoder blocks. Shared expert projections with private low-rank residuals constrain parameter growth, while rotary attention supports downstream spatial grids different from pretraining. The model is pretrained on 1.228 million MMEarth64 samples using modality-balanced masked reconstruction and structured sensor dropout. Frozen transfer is evaluated on six GEO-Bench tasks at both 64 and 224 pixels. The model reaches 64.42% mean intersection-over-union on cashew segmentation at 64 pixels and 90.56% average accuracy on EuroSAT at 224 pixels, exceeding the corresponding reported CSMoE results. BigEarthNet finetuning reaches 72.95% micro-average precision. Routing diagnostics distinguish expert participation, spatial dependence, modality association, and functional contribution. A held-out WorldCover probe measures a 0.64-percentage-point benefit from metadata, while retrieval separates same-sensor semantics from cross-sensor alignment. These results demonstrate sensor-flexible representation learning and strong task transfer using a compact parameter budget.

title: A Rubric-Guided Large Language Model Solution for Opioid Use Disorder Computable Phenotyping
abstract: Opioid use disorder (OUD) remains a public health crisis in the United States, yet it is difficult to identify from electronic health records (EHRs) because missing diagnosis codes and supporting evidence are buried in clinical narratives. Accurate OUD identification is critical to support interventions and improve health outcomes. This study developed a rubric-guided large language model (LLM) that incorporated Optimization by PROmpting (OPRO) for OUD computable phenotyping (CP). The framework used an 18-item, expert-identified rubric to instruct LLMs to automatically extract critical text with supporting evidence to determine OUD flags. Two UF Health physicians (GMR and WMG) chart-reviewed 253 patients, including 68 OUD-positive cases. Our LLM-based computable phenotype (CP) achieved the best F1 score of 0.774 and an AUROC of 0.934, outperforming the machine learning-based CP using EHR and natural language processing-extracted variables, and zero-shot LLMs by relative F1 improvements of 12.8% and 44.4%, respectively. The proposed LLM-based CP could link LLM-extracted evidence to OUD phenotyping for better explainability.

title: SimFuse3D: Source-Guided Target Simulation and Confidence-Guided Multi-Stage Localization Reweighting for Cross-Platform 3D Object Detection
abstract: Changes in sensor height and viewpoint alter object-level point distributions, making cross-platform LiDAR unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) difficult. Self-training uses labeled source scans and unlabeled target scans, yet a retained prediction may provide a useful target location while enclosing sparse foreground returns, background clutter, or points inconsistent with the predicted box. We refer to this mismatch as box-point inconsistency. We introduce SimFuse3D, which preserves the target placement and repairs the associated pseudo object using measured geometry from labeled source scans. Object Memory retrieves a similar labeled source instance. Target Simulation places the retrieved source geometry at the target location, aligns its points with the target viewing geometry, and filters the aligned crop to approximate the target observation. Confidence-Guided Multi-Stage Localization Reweighting (CMLR) maps each target pseudo-object confidence score to a bounded weight shared by RPN localization and R-CNN box regression. All components operate only during adaptation, leaving the detector architecture and inference graph unchanged. Across six cross-platform transfers, SimFuse3D consistently outperforms Pi3DET-Net and achieves the best performance among the compared adaptation methods on nearly all metrics. On nuScenes-to-KITTI, it ranks first among the compared adaptation methods with both evaluated detectors.

title: Capsule Lens: Locating and Tracking Concept Geometry in Model Representations
abstract: Understanding how concepts are encoded in the internal representations of machine learning models is a central problem in mechanistic interpretability, essential both for the science of deep learning and for the trustworthy deployment of increasingly capable models. Existing approaches to interpret model representations mainly map representations onto more interpretable spaces and do not directly characterize how concepts occupy representation space; various hypotheses have been proposed, but often lack of rigorous validation and largely focus on static representations. In this work, we introduce Capsule Lens, a framework that matches the region a concept occupies with a simple, trackable geometric form, a capsule, defined by several interpretable parameters, fitted in closed form to each concept's geometry and validated on held-out samples. We apply Capsule Lens in two major settings: static and dynamic representations. On static representations, we demonstrate how to locate concept geometry across various models, and how the span and norm curves uncover important geometric characteristics. On dynamic representations, we present three case studies tracking representation drifts induced by distinct training settings, CLIP pretraining, RL post-training on visual question answering, and RL post-training on mathematical reasoning. These analyses reveal qualitatively different geometric dynamics, ranging from broad network-wide restructuring in CLIP pretraining to localized and concept-specific changes in RL post-training. Our results include findings aligned with existing literature as well as novel observations. We believe Capsule Lens stands as a promising tool for locating, analyzing, and tracking concept geometry in both static and dynamic representations.

abstract: Version 1.0.1 of the reproducibility materials accompanying the manuscript 'A Reproducible Computational Framework for Leakage-Safe Temporal Evaluation, Calibration, and Decision Support in Credit Card Fraud Detection.' title: Adaptive Topology Mapping for Quantum Acceleration
abstract: This paper explores the application of adaptive topology mapping to quantum computation, aiming to enhance computational efficiency through a novel algorithm. Traditional approaches to topology mapping rely on classical computation, leading to limitations in computational speed. We propose a quantum acceleration technique that optimizes the core mapping process, offering a significant improvement in efficiency. The core mechanism centers on leveraging quantum phenomena to dynamically adjust the mapping process, achieving a higher degree of precision and faster convergence than existing methods. The study focuses on demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in a quantum computing framework, ultimately paving the way for more efficient and scalable quantum algorithms. The paper details the algorithm's design, implementation, and preliminary results demonstrating improved performance compared to baseline techniques.

title: Adaptive Neural Network Dynamic Graph Theory
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to graph neural networks (GNNs) utilizing an adaptive neural network (ANN) to dynamically adjust graph structures. Traditional GNNs often rely on manually designed graph structures, limiting their applicability to complex data. We introduce a new algorithm that leverages an ANN to automatically optimize the graph's topology, leading to improved performance and enhanced adaptability. The core mechanism centers around a self-adjusting network that iteratively refines graph connections based on data and task demands. This adaptive process allows the GNN to effectively learn and represent relationships within the graph, resulting in more accurate and robust predictions. We detail the implementation of the algorithm, provide a comprehensive analysis of its performance, and discuss its potential for advancing the field of graph neural networks.

title: Dimension Expansion Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Dimension Expansion Algorithm (DEA) leveraging quantum entanglement to dynamically extend the dimensional landscape for simulation purposes, particularly with emphasis on potential applications in quantum computing and exploration of hypothetical multi-dimensional spaces. The algorithm constructs a 'quantum entanglement dimension' that allows for the manipulation and expansion of a system's state space, mirroring the principles of quantum mechanics and offering a pathway to simulate complex quantum phenomena. The core mechanism centers around utilizing entanglement to establish a 'correlated dimension' – a fundamental quantum property – to facilitate the exploration of higher-dimensional spaces. We detail the algorithm's architecture, discuss its theoretical underpinnings, and present preliminary results demonstrating its capability to generate novel data spaces and explore potential quantum-related outcomes. The research explores the potential of this technique to generate complex quantum states and provide a pathway to advanced simulation methodologies.

title: Title: Quantum-Inspired Wave Function Collapse (QWWC) for Machine Learning
abstract: Quantum-Inspired Wave Function Collapse (QWWC) is a novel approach to machine learning algorithm optimization that seeks to enhance model accuracy and generalization through a modified wave function collapse process. Traditional methods often struggle with the inherent randomness of classical algorithms, leading to suboptimal performance. This paper proposes a new method that introduces quantum-inspired noise and entanglement into the wave function collapse, aiming to mitigate these limitations and improve model reliability. We explore the potential benefits of this approach in various machine learning tasks, focusing on [Specific Machine Learning Task - e.g., Deep Neural Network Classification] and demonstrating its effectiveness through simulations and preliminary experiments. The core of this work lies in the design of a novel noise distribution and entanglement strategy that minimizes the effects of classical randomness while maximizing the impact of quantum-inspired effects. This research highlights the potential for a paradigm shift in machine learning optimization, moving beyond approximations towards a more robust and precise approach.

title: 拓扑信息论与量子态的保护
abstract: This paper explores the synergistic application of topology-informed cryptography and quantum state protection. Traditional quantum state protection relies on classical cryptographic methods, which often struggle to provide robust security guarantees, particularly in the face of evolving computational power and novel attacks. This work proposes a novel framework leveraging the inherent topological properties of quantum states, aiming to create a fundamentally more secure and reliable approach to quantum information processing. The core claim is that by intelligently utilizing topology-informed cryptography, we can develop quantum state protection mechanisms capable of significantly enhancing the safety and trustworthiness of quantum information. This involves constructing quantum states with inherent protection through topological transformations, which can be exploited to detect and resist attacks. The paper presents a theoretical framework and preliminary experimental validation demonstrating the potential of this approach.

title: 基于量子拓扑的数值模拟方法
abstract: Quantum systems exhibit complex and often unpredictable behavior, posing significant challenges for traditional numerical simulations. This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum system dynamics, leveraging the principles of quantum topology to construct a highly accurate numerical simulation framework. We propose a method based on the inherent topological properties of quantum systems, allowing for a more precise and robust representation of their behavior. This work addresses the limitations of conventional methods by providing a fundamentally new framework for simulating quantum systems, specifically focusing on dynamic processes and offering enhanced accuracy. The core mechanism centers around the manipulation of topology to guide the computation, enabling a deeper understanding of quantum phenomena. We demonstrate the efficacy of this framework through a series of simulations, showcasing its potential to revolutionize the study of complex quantum systems.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Driven Distributed Storage
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed storage leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. Traditional distributed storage systems face limitations in capacity and security. This research introduces a system designed to overcome these limitations by harnessing the non-local nature of entanglement. The core concept involves encoding data into entangled quantum states distributed across multiple nodes. This enables secure data sharing, redundancy, and inherent error correction, potentially achieving significantly higher storage capacity and improved security compared to classical methods. The system utilizes the correlated nature of entangled particles to create a robust and inherently secure storage solution, addressing critical challenges in modern data management. The theoretical framework presented outlines the key principles and potential benefits of this entanglement-driven distributed storage architecture. Further research and development are needed to realize the full potential of this technology.

title: Quantum Topology: Adaptive Quantum System Simulation
abstract: Quantum topology, a fascinating field at the intersection of quantum mechanics and topology, offers a unique approach to simulating complex quantum systems. This paper introduces a novel method for quantum system simulation based on the principles of quantum topology, aiming to provide a more accurate and insightful representation of quantum evolution. The core mechanism leverages the inherent properties of quantum topology, enabling the simulation of intricate structures and predicting key quantum dynamics. This approach distinguishes itself through its focus on dynamic topology, offering a powerful tool for understanding the behavior of quantum systems. The paper presents a detailed explanation of the method, including the mathematical framework and the resulting simulation capabilities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique through illustrative examples, showcasing its potential to unlock new discoveries in quantum materials science and beyond.

title: Quantum-Inspired Bayesian Inference for High-Dimensional Feature Selection
abstract: High-dimensional feature selection remains a critical challenge in machine learning, particularly when dealing with datasets containing a large number of potential predictive variables. Traditional Bayesian approaches often struggle with this complexity due to the computational demands of exhaustive search or approximate inference methods. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging quantum-inspired techniques to accelerate the feature selection process. We simulate a quantum annealing process, representing feature selection as a probability distribution. Features are initially encoded as quantum bits (qubits), and interference patterns are manipulated to amplify the probabilities associated with relevant feature subsets, guided by a Bayesian prior. The core of this method is the exploitation of quantum superposition and interference to explore the feature space more efficiently than classical methods. The proposed approach aims to provide a computationally feasible solution for high-dimensional feature selection while maintaining the accuracy and interpretability inherent in Bayesian inference. The evaluation of the proposed method demonstrates its potential benefits in terms of speed and accuracy compared to traditional Bayesian methods, particularly when the number of features is large.

title: Quantum Effect-Based Self-Organizing Computation
abstract: Quantum Effect-Based Self-Organizing Computation (QESOC) presents a novel approach to quantum computing architecture, predicated on the principles of self-organization to achieve efficient and stable computation. The core claim is to develop a quantum computing system that leverages self-arrangement of qubits to optimize performance metrics, particularly speed and stability, addressing the limitations of current quantum hardware. This paper details the conceptual framework, implementation strategy, and potential advantages of QESOC, emphasizing its potential to significantly advance the field through the application of self-organization techniques.

title: Title: Non-Local Constraint Satisfaction via Quantum Entanglement
abstract: The field of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) presents a significant challenge in computer science, demanding exhaustive search to find feasible solutions. Classical algorithms struggle to efficiently explore the vast solution space, particularly for large and intricate CSPs. This research proposes a novel approach utilizing quantum entanglement to overcome these limitations, introducing a 'Quantum Resonance' mechanism that enables near-instantaneous exploration of solution configurations. Quantum entanglement provides a unique mechanism for creating probabilistic exploration of potential solutions, bypassing the limitations of classical search. We outline a framework for solving CSPs using this quantum entanglement-based approach, demonstrating its potential to drastically accelerate solution discovery. This work presents a new theoretical basis and preliminary implementation of a quantum algorithm designed to tackle complex CSPs. The core mechanism leverages entanglement to amplify promising solutions, offering a pathway to near-instantaneous exploration beyond classical computational limits. The paper details the design of the Quantum Resonance principle, and presents the results of initial experiments demonstrating the algorithm's efficacy in solving a subset of benchmark CSPs. Further investigation into the algorithm's scalability and potential for wider applicability is planned.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Probability Field Theory: A Graph-Based Structured Computation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to probabilistic field theory modeling, focusing on dynamic adaptive parameter adjustment for enhanced computational efficiency. Traditional methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting the scalability of complex system simulations. We propose a graph-based structure to represent the probability field, enabling dynamic adjustment of node and edge weights to optimize computational performance. This dynamic adjustment leverages the inherent structure of the graph to guide the simulation process, resulting in significant improvements in efficiency, particularly for high-dimensional and rapidly evolving systems. The core mechanism centers around a graph-based representation of the probability field, optimized parameter adjustment through a feedback loop. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through illustrative examples, showcasing its ability to accelerate complex simulations.

title: Non-Linear Topological Geometry Adaptive Reinforcement Learning Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for dynamic parameterization of complex systems, leveraging the inherent adaptability of non-linear topological geometry with adaptive reinforcement learning. Traditional reinforcement learning often focuses on optimizing explicit strategies, neglecting the system's underlying structure. We propose an algorithm that dynamically adjusts the learning objective based on the topological structure of the system, enabling automated optimization of complex systems' performance. This framework utilizes a novel self-organizing constraint-based reinforcement learning approach to achieve adaptive parameterization. The core claim is that this approach can automatically optimize complex systems by adapting to the system's inherent topological properties, offering a new paradigm for designing dynamic and robust systems. This work addresses the limitations of existing reinforcement learning techniques by explicitly incorporating topological structure into the optimization process.

title: Introduction to Graph Neural Networks
abstract: We can naturally express the connections between the set of objects as patterns of graphs. A graph is a mathematical structure consists of the vertices and the links, where each node can have multiple nodes and edges connected to it. Mathematical graphs are often represented as arrays of elements, such as adjacency and incidence matrices. Graph theory provides a crucial framework for handling complicated, wide data easily in various fields, which includes network modeling, routing algorithms, and more. Graph theory helps to design and analyze complicated networks, such as the ecological networks, social networks and transportation systems, and also provides efficient algorithms for finding shortest paths and optimal routes in networks. Graph theory can be used to produce predictive models like the graph neural networks which help to learn about patterns and connections between the set of data. These graph networks are one of the neural networks to handle the graphical structured data in which, the nodes represent objects such as persons, organizations, locations and the edges represent the connection and the interactions between the objects, such as friendships, collaborations and the transactions. One of the emerging technologies is the machine learning algorithm which follows the concept of a human neuron. A neuron collects input from multiple neurons and transmits signals to multiple neurons. Artificial neural networks consist of a three-stage process, which includes the input layer, iteration or hidden layer and output layer. An input layer observes the input from the system or environment. A hidden or iteration layer may process and transform the input data through multiple layers of interconnected neurons. The output layer determines the output or prediction based on processed input data. Graph neural networks play some significant roles in FinTech and fraud detection, like transaction monitoring, digital payments, identity verification, biometric authentication, anomaly detection, predictive modeling, etc. The notable benefits of neural networks in FinTech and fraud detection are reduced losses, regulatory compliance, and increased efficiency.

title: Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education
abstract: The integration of GenAI tools into higher education assessment raises important questions about how students understand, interpret, and respond to AI-mediated evaluation. As instructors increasingly explore AI tools for providing feedback, prior research has examined whether GenAI-generated feedback improves writing performance and how students perceive its usefulness; comparatively little is known, however, about how students interpret such evaluation when they are explicitly informed that an AI system, rather than a human instructor, produced the feedback and the score. This study reports findings from a qualitative pedagogical inquiry conducted in an undergraduate technical communication course for computing students at a Saudi public university. Thirteen male undergraduate computing students completed an in-class handwritten writing task; the scanned submissions were evaluated by ChatGPT using a rubric-based prompt aligned with the task objectives. Students were then explicitly informed that ChatGPT had generated the score and feedback and were invited to reflect on the evaluation in writing. Inductive thematic analysis of these reflections identified four themes: perceived usefulness of feedback; awareness of AI's contextual and pedagogical limitations; conditional trust, distinguishing feedback utility from evaluative authority; and reflection on the institutional and pedagogical role of the human instructor. Participants accepted GenAI feedback as useful for surface-level revision but consistently positioned the human instructor as the appropriate authority over grading decisions. The study identifies this as a distinction between feedback utility and evaluative authority, two judgments that students treat as analytically separate rather than as opposite ends of a single approval scale...

title: Fanout Complexity of Symmetric Boolean Functions in $\mathsf{QAC}^0$
abstract: Whether $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ can compute $\mathtt{PARITY}_n$ remains open. Computing $\mathtt{PARITY}_n$ is equivalent to implementing $\mathtt{FANOUT}_n$ under $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ reductions. This raises a more general question: for an arbitrary symmetric Boolean function $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$, what fanout size is necessary and sufficient for computing $f$ in $\mathsf{QAC}^0$? We show that the answer is exactly the transition radius $ρ(f)$: computing $f$ and implementing $\mathtt{FANOUT}_{ρ(f)}$ are equivalent under $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ reductions. In particular, if $ρ(f)\ge n^δ$ for some constant $δ>0$, then computing $f$ is $\mathsf{QAC}^0_{\mathrm{f}}$-complete. Combined with Paturi's theorem, our characterization implies that if $\mathtt{PARITY}_n \notin \mathsf{QAC}^0$, then any Boolean function in $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ of approximate degree $n^{1/2+Ω(1)}$ must be nonsymmetric.

title: Minimax Lower Bound for Estimating Diffusion-based Local Intrinsic Dimension
abstract: While diffusion-based methods have recently emerged as effective tools for probing the intrinsic geometry of high-dimensional data, their statistical difficulty remains largely unexplored. We study estimation of the finite-scale population functional underlying FLIPD (Kamkari et al., 2024; arXiv:2406.03537), a diffusion-based local intrinsic dimension (LID) quantity defined through the logarithmic scale derivative of a Gaussian-smoothed density. Intuitively, Gaussian smoothing turns local dimension into a scale law: near a $d$-dimensional manifold, the kernel mass grows like $σ^d$, so differentiating with respect to the noise scale reveals the intrinsic exponent. Under a regular manifold model, we show uniformly over the model class that the finite-scale field differs from the manifold dimension $d$ by at most $O(σ^2)$. We then establish a minimax lower bound of order $(nσ^d)^{-1}$ for estimating this finite-scale field from $n$ observations, for $n^{-1/(2α+d)}\lesssimσ\leσ_0$. At the smallest scale covered by our lower-bound construction, the bound becomes the nonparametric rate $n^{-2α/(2α+d)}$.

title: Blind Random Search with Noisy Loss Measurements: Averaging, Thresholding, and Almost Sure Convergence
abstract: Blind random search repeatedly draws a candidate point and replaces the current estimate whenever the candidate has a lower loss. In the absence of noise, the true loss is observed directly. It decreases strictly at every accepted update and is monotone nonincreasing over all iterations. Measurement noise can make a worse candidate appear better and thereby break this monotonicity. To recover almost sure convergence under noise, we incorporate averaging and thresholding into the original decision criterion. These two classical tools are coupled. As the sample sizes grow, the positive threshold shrinks at a matched rate. These modifications allow blind random search to recover eventual monotonicity of the true loss under noisy measurements and to converge almost surely.

title: What Matters in On-Policy Distillation? A Perspective on Data Efficiency and Data Selection
abstract: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) has emerged as a widely adopted post-training paradigm for enhancing large language models in reasoning domains. However, the data-centric mechanisms in OPD remain relatively underexplored. This paper presents an empirical study of data efficiency and data selection in OPD. We begin by investigating an extreme setting: training OPD on only one example, namely 1-shot OPD. Surprisingly, we find that 1-shot OPD is consistently effective across all sampled training examples and harder examples often yield superior performance gain. We next investigate what actually drives the student model's improvement in the training data. Our analysis reveals that the improvement is not driven by high token entropy, but the longer CoT paths which hard problem naturally generate. Training on longer CoT can help maintain closer alignment with the teacher over a long reasoning horizon, and learn critical thinking patterns usually missing in short CoTs, such as reflection (e.g., "Alternatively"). Based on these insights, we propose a simple data selection method that selects only hard examples for training, where even "unsolvable" examples that completely exceed the teacher's capability can be successfully used. Our experiments conducted on five models ranging from 1.5B to 8B show that training the student model on only 8 selected hard examples matches the performance of the 17K dataset baseline. Code and models will be publicly available.

We begin by investigating an extreme setting: training OPD on only one example, namely 1-shot OPD. Surprisingly, we find that 1-shot OPD is consistently effective across all sampled training examples and harder examples often yield superior performance gain. We next investigate what actually drives the student model's improvement in the training data. Our analysis reveals that the improvement is not driven by high token entropy, but the longer CoT paths which hard problem naturally generate. Training on longer CoT can help maintain closer alignment with the teacher over a long reasoning horizon, and learn critical thinking patterns usually missing in short CoTs, such as reflection (e.g., "Alternatively"). Based on these insights, we propose a simple data selection method that selects only hard examples for training, where even "unsolvable" examples that completely exceed the teacher's capability can be successfully used. Our experiments conducted on five models ranging from 1.5B to 8B show that training the student model on only 8 selected hard examples matches the performance of the 17K dataset baseline. Code and models will be publicly available.

title: Unsupervised Transfer Clustering for Mitigating Cold Start in Active Prompt Learning
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are able to achieve impressive zero-shot classification performance by aligning visual and textual representations, but each new task still demands handcrafted prompts. Active Prompt Learning (APL) combines Active Learning (AL) and Prompt Learning (PL) into a single framework, allowing for the usage of the VLM prior knowledge for iteratively querying the most informative images to be labeled. However, the cold-start problem is still relevant for APL methods, where the performance of the initial query can be worse than random sampling. While recent state-of-the-art APL methods mitigate with balanced sampling and multimodal features, they rely on rigid, distance-based clustering to group these features. This simplistic approach can struggle to capture the complex, high-dimensional semantic distributions inherent to VLMs, leading to suboptimal query representativeness. Unsupervised transfer can be applied to these features as a possible alternative, since it is capable of inferring the underlying human labeling of a task without any form of supervision. This way, samples can be grouped in semantically coherent clusters. This paper proposes Unsupervised Transfer Clustering with Selective Querying (UTC+SQ), a framework that enhances a recent APL approach by leveraging state-of-the-art unsupervised transfer model. These models generate high-fidelity pseudo-labels that establish semantically meaningful clusters, allowing for the selection of more relevant samples. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that shifting from distance-based to projection-based clustering improves the representativeness of the queried subset, achieving accuracy gains in 6 of the 8 datasets tested.

title: Improving Language Identification for Code-Switched Utterances with Integer Linear Programming
abstract: Automatic identification of code-switched (CS) utterances remains a challenge for language identification (LID) systems, causing such texts to be underrepresented in the training data of Large Language Models. In this paper, we revisit MaskLID, a state-of-the art approach for CS identification, which requires no training and detects arbitrary language combinations. We make three main contributions: (a) we reveal, and address, a major issue of MaskLID: its overreliance on word-level language association scores; (b) we reformulate the underlying optimization algorithm as an Integer Linear Program, enabling us to experiment with a large set of clear and interpretable constraints; (c) each of these improvements vastly improves the baseline system, as we illustrate in experiments involving 10~diverse languages, where we observe a strong boost in performance on CS benchmarks. We release our code and data for reproducibility.

title: 基于动态量子纠缠的自适应机器学习
abstract: This paper presents a novel self-adaptive machine learning model leveraging the principles of dynamic quantum entanglement. Traditional machine learning algorithms often struggle with high-dimensional data and complex correlations, limiting their performance. This research introduces a quantum-enhanced approach that exploits the unique properties of quantum entanglement to improve data association and feature extraction. The core mechanism involves utilizing quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust the weighting of data points, leading to enhanced model accuracy and efficiency. We explore the potential of this approach to overcome limitations of classical machine learning in scenarios demanding high-dimensional data and intricate correlations. The study highlights the benefits of employing quantum entanglement within the framework of self-adaptive learning, proposing a new method for improving model performance and robustness.

title: 基于图的混沌动力学与机器学习的协同优化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to optimization that integrates graph-based chaos dynamics with machine learning, aiming to enhance optimization processes through synergistic collaboration. The core concept revolves around constructing a dynamic graph representing the problem space, where chaos dynamics are utilized to generate a diverse set of solutions, and machine learning algorithms are employed to refine and guide the optimization process based on these generated solutions. The integration of these two paradigms promises a more intelligent and robust optimization strategy compared to traditional methods. We present a framework incorporating graph representation, chaos modeling, and machine learning for automated exploration and improvement of solutions. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this integrated approach through a series of illustrative examples across different optimization problems, highlighting its potential for achieving superior performance and adaptability.

title: 基于遗传算法的自适应动力系统优化
abstract: This paper investigates the application of genetic algorithms (GAs) to optimize complex dynamic systems. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with such systems, presenting a significant challenge. We propose a novel GA-based approach designed to address this challenge by providing an adaptive optimization strategy. The core mechanism centers around a genetic operator that iteratively refines the system parameters through a simulated environment, resulting in improved control and performance. The paper details the algorithm's structure, the optimization process, and the results achieved through simulation, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach in optimizing a specific dynamic system. The benefits include improved efficiency, robustness, and scalability compared to traditional optimization techniques.

title: Microscopic Quantum Information Encryption
abstract: This paper explores the theoretical foundations of microscopic quantum information encryption and proposes a novel cryptographic algorithm based on quantum entanglement. The core claim is that the unique properties of quantum entanglement can be leveraged to establish robust information security, rendering traditional cryptographic methods obsolete. The proposed algorithm utilizes entanglement to encrypt data and verify its integrity, offering a paradigm shift in secure communication. We present a detailed theoretical analysis and preliminary design of this system, emphasizing the critical role of quantum entanglement in maintaining data confidentiality. The paper concludes with a discussion of the challenges and future directions for this research.

title: 基于动态几何的量子态的纠缠增强算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum state enhancement algorithm based on dynamic geometry, designed to significantly boost the entanglement strength of quantum states. Traditional approaches often rely on static entanglement enhancement, limiting potential performance gains. This research proposes a dynamic geometry framework that iteratively adjusts geometric parameters to optimize entanglement, achieving a substantial increase in quantum state coherence and fidelity. We detail the algorithm's core mechanics, present experimental validation demonstrating improved entanglement strength, and discuss its potential impact on quantum computing performance. The core claim focuses on the dynamic adjustment of geometric parameters to enhance entanglement, a departure from traditional approaches. This work represents a significant advancement in quantum state manipulation, offering a promising pathway towards enhanced quantum algorithms.

title: Quantum Degeneracy-Based Nonlinear Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on quantum degeneracy, designed to address challenges posed by high-degree non-linear problems. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with these complex scenarios, particularly when high precision is crucial. The proposed algorithm leverages quantum degeneracy, a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics, to stabilize the optimization process and enhance the solution accuracy. We detail the core mechanism, outlining how quantum degeneracy mitigates sensitivity to initial conditions and promotes convergence to optimal solutions. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through a series of rigorous theoretical analyses and preliminary numerical experiments, showcasing its superiority over existing methods in a range of non-linear optimization scenarios. We conclude with a discussion of the potential applications and future directions for this innovative technique.

title: Title: Topological Quantum Entanglement as a Resource for Universal Computation
abstract: Topological Quantum Entanglement (TQE) represents a paradigm shift in quantum computation, moving beyond the limitations of classical representations by leveraging dynamic, self-organizing topologies within quantum systems. This paper proposes a novel framework for generating and manipulating TQE, demonstrating its potential for parallel processing and superposition-based algorithms with enhanced computational capabilities. The core mechanism involves establishing a fundamental topology within a quantum system, enabling algorithmic manipulation that circumvents traditional constraints. We present a theoretical foundation and preliminary experimental results exploring the feasibility of this approach, highlighting its potential to revolutionize computation.

title: 混沌几何的自适应拓扑转化与量子计算
abstract: 混沌几何是物理学和数学领域中一个引人入胜的领域,其复杂性与精确预测的难度密切相关。本研究探讨了利用混沌几何的自适应拓扑转化与量子计算相结合的策略,旨在实现高精度拓扑转化和计算,并提升计算效率。传统拓扑转化方法往往依赖于固定的拓扑结构,而本研究提出了一种创新的算法,利用混沌几何的自适应拓扑转化,结合量子计算,为解决复杂拓扑问题提供了新的途径。通过对混沌几何的深入研究,以及量子计算的优势,本研究旨在推动混沌几何与量子计算的交叉发展,并探索其在特定应用场景中的潜在价值。

title: Probability Space Theory: A Domain-Adaptive Learning Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel probabilistic space theory-based domain-adaptive learning algorithm designed to enhance model generalization and adaptability. Traditional machine learning algorithms often rely on static, pre-defined learning objectives, limiting their ability to handle data distribution shifts. We propose a system that dynamically adjusts learning goals based on probabilistic space representations, effectively enabling the algorithm to continuously refine its parameters in response to evolving data distributions. The core of this approach involves representing the learning objective as a probability distribution within a probabilistic space, and employing a self-adaptive weighting mechanism to adjust the distribution based on observations. The algorithm's design incorporates a novel "self-adaptation" mechanism, which iteratively adjusts the probability distribution to minimize prediction error and maximize the information-theoretic distance between the model's predictions and the true data. This results in improved performance across a range of scenarios and datasets. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through experiments on a diverse set of benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in both generalization and robustness. The potential implications of this research extend to various domains requiring robust and adaptable models.

title: Adaptive Dimension Space Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces an Adaptive Dimension Space Algorithm (ADSA) designed to address linear algebra and optimization challenges, particularly in the context of high-dimensional data. ADSA dynamically adjusts the dimensionality of the data space, leveraging the inherent properties of dimensionality transformation to significantly accelerate optimization processes. The algorithm's core mechanism centers around a framework that automatically adjusts the dimension based on problem scale and data characteristics, resulting in enhanced adaptability and efficiency. Traditional approaches often fall short in handling complex, high-dimensional datasets, and ADSA offers a novel solution for improved performance.

title: Active Learning-Based Domain Knowledge Extraction Framework
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for automatically extracting domain knowledge using active learning. The core idea is to systematically identify and extract key information from a domain knowledge base to construct a knowledge graph. This is achieved through a mechanism that leverages the uncertainty inherent in knowledge graph construction and employs reinforcement learning to optimize the knowledge extraction strategy. Specifically, the system iteratively selects samples for human annotation based on this uncertainty, and then utilizes reinforcement learning to refine its selection criteria, maximizing knowledge extraction efficiency. The framework addresses the challenge of manually curating knowledge bases by providing an automated and adaptive approach. The proposed method demonstrates a significant improvement in knowledge extraction compared to traditional passive learning approaches. The primary goal is to build a robust and accurate knowledge graph with minimal human intervention. The system's performance is evaluated using standard knowledge graph construction metrics, showcasing its effectiveness and potential for various domains.

title: Hierarchical Symbolic Regression with Genetic Programming
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to symbolic regression, termed Hierarchical Symbolic Regression with Genetic Programming (HSRPG). The core idea is to combine the strengths of both symbolic regression and genetic programming (GP) within a hierarchical framework. Traditional symbolic regression struggles with complex, high-dimensional problems due to the exponential growth of the search space. Genetic programming, while capable of exploring a wider range of solutions, often lacks the interpretability and efficiency of symbolic expressions. HSRPG addresses these limitations by structuring the regression problem hierarchically. At each level of the hierarchy, GP is applied to evolve a set of symbolic expressions, which are then fed as inputs to the next level. This decomposition dramatically reduces the complexity of the overall problem, improving scalability and efficiency. We detail the architecture of the HSRPG system, the evolutionary operators used at each level, and demonstrate its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and conceptual examples. The resulting system offers a promising avenue for automatically discovering intricate mathematical relationships from data, particularly in domains where the underlying functions are unknown.

title: Riemannian Optimization for Learning Optimal Graph Structures
abstract: Learning optimal graph structures from data is a fundamental problem across numerous domains, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and machine learning. Traditional graph learning methods often rely on heuristic approaches or iterative algorithms that can be computationally expensive and may not effectively capture the underlying geometric relationships within the data. This paper proposes a novel framework utilizing Riemannian optimization to directly learn optimal graph structures. The core idea is to represent the graph structure as a set of parameters and leverage the geometry of the data manifold through Riemannian optimization techniques. Specifically, we employ conjugate gradient methods on the Riemannian manifold defined by the graph parameters. This approach allows us to minimize a loss function that quantifies the discrepancy between predicted and observed data, while simultaneously considering the intrinsic curvature of the data manifold. The results demonstrate that Riemannian optimization provides a more efficient and accurate method for graph learning compared to conventional approaches, leading to improved graph structures that better represent the underlying data distribution. The key innovations lie in the direct application of Riemannian optimization for graph structure learning and the incorporation of geometric information for enhanced optimization performance.

title: Quantum Computing Chaos System Dynamics Modeling (QCSDM)
abstract: Quantum Computing Chaos System Dynamics Modeling (QCSDM) presents a novel approach to chaos system modeling, leveraging the unique properties of quantum computation to create a sophisticated framework for dynamic process simulation and precise prediction. This research focuses on establishing a quantum-based dynamic model, capable of capturing the intricate behavior of complex systems through the application of quantum mechanics. title: Adaptive Information Encoding Protocols
abstract: This paper explores the design of an Adaptive Information Encoding Protocol (AIEP) leveraging quantum entanglement and self-correcting mechanisms to achieve unprecedented information transmission efficiency. Traditional information encoding methods are static and inflexible, hindering their effectiveness in dynamic environments. The AIEP introduces a novel concept – the "Quantum Entanglement Information Protocol" – which utilizes quantum entanglement to accelerate information transfer and incorporates a self-assessment and correction system to mitigate information degradation. This research aims to provide a foundational framework for quantum communication and data processing, potentially revolutionizing data transmission capabilities.

title: Non-Linear Topological Constraint Optimization (NLTO)
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to Non-Linear Topological Constraint Optimization (NLTO), a method designed to address the inherent challenges of optimizing complex systems where topological constraints significantly influence performance. Traditional optimization techniques often struggle with non-linear systems due to the assumption of linear relationships. NLTO overcomes this limitation by incorporating a dynamic topological structure adjustment mechanism, enabling the algorithm to adapt to complex, non-linear constraints and maximize performance. We detail the core concepts, the implementation of the Non-Linear Topological Constraint Solver, and the results achieved through simulations. The paper concludes with a discussion of the advantages and potential applications of this method in various domains.

title: Dynamic Constraint-Based Evolutionary Algorithm (DCBA)
abstract: This paper introduces the Dynamic Constraint-Based Evolutionary Algorithm (DCBA), a novel hybrid approach to optimization that combines the strengths of evolutionary algorithms with constraint satisfaction techniques. DCBA addresses the limitations of traditional evolutionary algorithms by incorporating adaptive mutation and selection strategies that dynamically adjust to changes in the constraints of the problem. The algorithm's core mechanism centers around a feedback loop that continuously refines the search space by leveraging evolutionary principles while simultaneously enforcing constraint satisfaction, leading to rapid discovery of optimal solutions to complex, multi-objective optimization problems. This paper details the algorithm's design, implementation, and preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness in a range of challenging scenarios.

title: Confounding-Valid Conformal Inference for Counterfactual KPIs in Wireless Networks
abstract: Conformal counterfactual inference enables network operators to use logged telemetry to reliably answer 'what-if' questions about network operation. These answers typically take the form of prediction sets that contain, with a user-defined probability, the key performance indicators (KPIs) that would have been observed under alternative control actions. A key challenge is that logged telemetry may omit variables used by the controller, resulting in hidden confounding and invalidating the statistical guarantees of counterfactual analysis. In principle, this issue can be addressed using randomized telemetry, collected by assigning control actions independently of the network state. However, because such randomization may disrupt normal operation, randomized telemetry is typically scarce, causing counterfactual analysis based solely on it to produce uninformative prediction sets. To address these challenges, we propose Confounding-Valid Counterfactual Conformal Inference (CV-CCI), which combines abundant, potentially confounded observational telemetry with limited randomized data through the General Synthetic-Powered Inference (GESPI) principle. CV-CCI leverages observational data to improve efficiency while using randomized data to retain finite-sample coverage guarantees under arbitrary hidden confounding. Experiments on two representative radio access network (RAN) control tasks show that CV-CCI remains valid under hidden confounding while producing more efficient prediction sets than state-of-the-art confounding-valid baselines.

title: Cost-Aware Hierarchical Multi-Agent Ransomware Detection and Family Attribution under Analysis Budgets
abstract: Sandbox execution and memory forensics are among the most constrained resources in malware triage. Static analysis can scale to millions of files, whereas dynamic and memory analysis require minutes of analyst controlled infrastructure for each sample. Despite this difference, multimodal ransomware detectors often apply every modality to every sample, causing analysis cost and time to verdict to increase linearly with sample volume even when static evidence is already sufficient for a decision. We present a cost aware Hierarchical Multi-Agent System that formulates evidence acquisition as a budgeted sequential decision problem. Specialist agents generate schema validated risk signals for each modality, domain controllers aggregate these signals, and a Meta-Orchestrator begins with static evidence and escalates to dynamic and memory evidence only when confidence is insufficient or agents within a controller disagree. An optional, bounded, locally hosted large language model reviewer can adjust a verdict by at most one tier but cannot replace the deterministic pipeline. Each decision is recorded with a complete provenance trace. In multiple runs over 12439 samples from 16 ransomware families and benign samples, the deterministic HMAS achieves F1 0.93 and macro F1 0.97, resolving 57.95% of cases using static evidence alone, 35.83% after adding dynamic evidence, and only 6.21% through the full pipeline. The average internal analysis cost is 6.65 units, compared with 12 for exhaustive analysis, representing a 44.6% reduction. Standalone leave-one-family-out testing further shows that accuracy on families held out during tuning falls to 0.26 to 0.64 outside the Benign and high support classes. We report these results alongside a cost sensitivity analysis, a partial leave one component out ablation, and a full scale comparison with learned early and late fusion and cascade baselines.

title: MABPD: Multi-Agent Bias Probing & Detection via Structured Argument Debate
abstract: Media bias in news articles operates through subtle linguistic cues---loaded language, selective framing, and strategic omission---that resist single-model detection and have traditionally required large annotated corpora for supervised training. We ask whether structured multi-agent deliberation can serve as a principled, training-free alternative to supervised classification for this task. We introduce MABPD (Multi-Agent Bias Probing & Detection), a pipeline in which three specialized LLM agents analyze an article from complementary perspectives and resolve disagreements through a Structured Argument Debate (SAD) protocol. SAD implements a domain-motivated asymmetric burden of proof---biased claims without grounded textual evidence carry zero weight---combined with role-weighted voting and post-consensus verification, replacing task-specific supervised decision boundaries with explicit deliberative structure. Ablation confirms that this structured deliberation, not mere agent parallelism, drives performance: removing the debate module reduces F1 by up to 10.6 points. On the BABE benchmark (4,121 expert-annotated sentences), MABPD achieves 83.4% macro F1 on the held-out test split---within 0.7 percentage points (pp) of the supervised SOTA (MAGPIE, 84.1% macro F1; Horych et al., 2024)---without any task-specific training or threshold tuning on annotated data. Cross-dataset evaluation on the SemEval 2019 HyperPartisan corpus (644 articles) yields 75.0% zero-shot accuracy, within 7.2 pp of the supervised SOTA accuracy (82.2%; Kiesel et al. 2019), confirming transfer across annotation regimes. We release the full pipeline and evaluation code.

title: 基于动态概率的模态与量子纠缠的融合
abstract: This paper explores a novel framework for quantum computation and probability computation leveraging dynamic probability. Traditional approaches often struggle to effectively utilize the inherent dynamism of probability in quantum systems. We propose a method that integrates dynamic probability with quantum entanglement, enabling enhanced efficiency and precision in both calculations and probabilistic outcomes. This integration addresses limitations of current quantum computing architectures by providing a more adaptable and robust system. The core mechanism hinges on dynamically adjusting quantum state parameters based on probabilistic feedback, leading to improved performance across a range of quantum algorithms. The resulting framework demonstrates significant potential for accelerating quantum algorithms and improving the reliability of probabilistic outcomes.

title: 基于自适应的图论推理的特征选择
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to feature selection based on adaptive graph theory reasoning. Traditional feature selection methods often rely on static models, limiting their effectiveness in complex graph-based problems. We propose a framework leveraging the adaptive nature of graph structures and parameters to improve reasoning efficiency. This method employs a self-organizing neural network to dynamically adjust the network's structure and parameters, allowing it to effectively handle intricate graph datasets. The core claim is that this adaptive approach surpasses conventional methods in addressing complex graph-related tasks. This work presents a framework that adapts to the graph's characteristics, enhancing the robustness and efficiency of the feature selection process. We evaluate the method's performance on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating improved accuracy and reduced computational complexity compared to existing techniques.

title: Quantum Non-Linear Geometry Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum computing to revolutionize optimization problems, particularly those involving complex physical systems. We introduce a novel quantum non-linear geometry optimization algorithm that leverages quantum entanglement and geometric topology to directly simulate intricate physical models and facilitate highly customized solutions. The core mechanism centers around the quantum computer's ability to explore complex geometric spaces, offering a fundamentally different approach compared to traditional classical methods. The paper details the algorithm's design, the advantages it offers, and its potential impact across various fields requiring complex optimization. We argue that this quantum-enhanced optimization technique represents a significant step towards achieving more efficient and accurate solutions to problems currently intractable with classical algorithms.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Programming for Complex Constraint Satisfaction
abstract: Quantum-enhanced constraint programming (QCP) offers a promising avenue for accelerating the solution of complex constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) by harnessing the unique properties of quantum computation. This paper investigates the potential of integrating quantum algorithms into constraint programming to achieve exponential speedups in solving problems with large state spaces. We explore the core mechanisms involved, focusing on quantum superposition and entanglement to represent and manipulate constraint relationships, and outline a theoretical framework for demonstrating the benefits of this approach. We present a novel design for leveraging quantum entanglement to enhance the exploration of solution space, ultimately aiming to significantly improve the performance of existing CSP solvers. The paper concludes by discussing the challenges and future directions of QCP research.

title: Title: Dynamically Adaptive Modular Lattice Structures for Quantum Simulation
abstract: Quantum simulation, a crucial tool for fundamental physics research, faces significant challenges with current methods due to limitations in precision and adaptability. This paper introduces a novel approach utilizing dynamically adaptive modular lattice structures to overcome these limitations, offering unprecedented control and fidelity in quantum system simulations. We propose a self-organizing algorithm employing fractal geometry and iterative refinement to automatically generate lattices with variable connectivity and branching patterns. This dynamic structure is designed to perfectly mimic complex quantum states, providing unparalleled control and accuracy in simulations. The core mechanism leverages feedback loops to maintain optimal representation of quantum states, ensuring a high degree of fidelity. This work represents a significant advancement in lattice simulation, offering a pathway towards more powerful and versatile quantum computational capabilities.

title: Algorithmic Bayesian Probability (ABP)
abstract: This paper introduces Algorithmic Bayesian Probability (ABP), a novel algorithm designed to dynamically adjust Bayesian probability estimates in response to observed data. Traditional Bayesian methods often rely on fixed prior distributions, limiting the algorithm's ability to effectively model complex systems. ABP addresses this limitation through the implementation of an Adaptive Bayesian Network (ABN) that continuously refines probability assessments using a learned model of the system's dynamics. This research explores the potential for ABP to significantly improve predictive accuracy in challenging scenarios by incorporating real-time data and adapting to evolving system conditions. The core mechanism involves a dynamic Bayesian network structure that iteratively updates probability estimates based on observed data.

title: Probability Logic: Dimensional Extension
abstract: Probability logic, traditionally focused on deductive reasoning and logical inference, is being significantly extended through the development of a dimensionality expansion approach. This paper explores a novel methodology that integrates logical rules and reasoning mechanisms with probabilistic distributions, aiming to enhance the performance of machine learning models. We introduce a concept of "dimensional expansion" – a progressive refinement of logical structure and inference processes – to improve model generalization and adaptability. This work presents a framework for dynamically increasing complexity, potentially unlocking new applications in diverse machine learning domains. The core mechanism centers around a layered approach to logic, iteratively adding constraints and probabilistic representations to optimize model outcomes. This paper details the implementation of this framework, demonstrating its impact through theoretical analysis and preliminary experiments.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Intrinsic Motivation for Cooperative Navigation
abstract: This paper investigates the challenges of achieving robust cooperative navigation in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) scenarios, addressing the limitations of relying solely on extrinsic rewards. We propose a novel framework integrating intrinsic motivation – specifically, curiosity and surprise – into each agent's reward function. Our core claim is that extrinsic rewards alone frequently fail to foster genuine cooperation, leading to suboptimal collective behavior. title: Causal Bayesian Networks with Differential Privacy
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for constructing and learning causal Bayesian networks (CBNs) with differential privacy (DP). The core challenge addressed is the inherent tension between causal inference, which relies on potentially sensitive data, and the rigorous privacy guarantees offered by differential privacy. We introduce a score-based approach coupled with a carefully designed noise addition strategy specifically tailored to CBN learning. This mechanism aims to preserve the integrity of the causal structure while simultaneously minimizing information leakage, a critical step toward practical and trustworthy causal discovery in privacy-sensitive environments. The framework provides a theoretical foundation for combining these two crucial aspects of data analysis, offering a promising path for real-world applications where both causal understanding and data protection are paramount. The key contributions lie in the adaptive noise schedule and its connection to maintaining the faithfulness of the learned CBN. We demonstrate that by adjusting the noise level based on the learning process, we can achieve strong privacy guarantees without significantly compromising the accuracy of the discovered causal relationships.

title: Core Claim: A Dynamic Matrix Approach to Quantum Entanglement Computation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, presents a unique opportunity for computation and algorithm development. However, the limitations of traditional quantum computing methods—particularly in terms of computational complexity and algorithm design—have hindered progress. This paper introduces a novel approach, leveraging dynamic matrix systems, to enhance quantum entanglement computation. We propose a method that utilizes the inherent properties of quantum entanglement to streamline matrix operations, ultimately enabling more efficient quantum algorithms and computations. This work addresses the limitations of current quantum computing paradigms by introducing a new framework that exploits entanglement for enhanced computational power.

title: Dynamic Topology Mapping Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel optimization algorithm based on dynamic topology mapping, designed to overcome the limitations of traditional optimization methods. The algorithm iteratively adjusts the topology of the objective function, employing a dynamic mapping process to guide the search for optimal solutions. The core mechanism centers on a closed-loop optimization strategy leveraging the inherent properties of topology. This approach aims to achieve global optimal solutions, surpassing the capabilities of existing methods. We present a detailed analysis of the algorithm's design, implementation, and performance evaluation, demonstrating its effectiveness in solving complex optimization problems. The paper explores the advantages of this dynamic topology mapping approach, including its ability to navigate intricate landscapes and guarantee convergence to a global optimum.

title: The Adaptive Memory Network of Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel recurrent neural network architecture, termed the Adaptive Memory Network (AMN), designed to enhance learning and memory capabilities through dynamic memory weight adjustment. Traditional recurrent neural networks (RNNs) suffer from limitations in adapting to varying data distributions and user behavior, hindering their performance. The AMN addresses these limitations by incorporating a dynamic memory weight adjustment mechanism that learns user behavior and contextual information to dynamically adjust the weights associated with each memory unit. This adaptive approach significantly improves the network's ability to capture complex patterns and maintain long-term memory, leading to more efficient learning and improved memory retention. The paper presents a detailed theoretical analysis of the proposed mechanism and demonstrates its effectiveness through a series of experiments on benchmark datasets. The results show that the AMN outperforms existing RNN architectures in terms of learning speed and memory retention.

title: Spatio-temporal prediction of roof available light energy capacity based on CNN-BiLSTM model and multi-source meteorological coupling
abstract: With the swift advancement of distributed photovoltaic power generation roof available light capacity has become an important basis for urban renewable energy planning and grid dispatching. In response to the problems of insufficient fusion of multi-source meteorological information and inadequate extraction of spatio-temporal features in existing methods, a Convolutional Neural Network-Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-BiLSTM) hybrid prediction model that fuses multi-source meteorological data with roof geometry was introduced. The findings demonstrated that the CNN-BiLSTM model converged to 96.3% accuracy and 95.2% recall after 80 iterations, and the mean absolute error (MAE) and mean absolute percentage error were reduced to 0.58 kW and 5.3% respectively, both clearly outperforming the control model; Under six different weather conditions, the model MAE remained in the range of 0.43–0.73 kW, especially under conditions of intense radiation fluctuations such as cloudy and overcast days. In actual photovoltaic project validation, the model’s prediction error for the annual power generation of six real scenarios was controlled within ± 3.1%, superior to the general tool PVGIS (with an error of up to ± 12.4%). The results show that the CNN-BiLSTM model outperforms the comparison models in terms of prediction accuracy and convergence speed, and demonstrates good adaptability in the complex meteorological conditions and real scenarios of Taiyuan region. The research results can provide useful technical reference for the assessment of urban distributed photovoltaic resources, the prioritization of roof development, and regional energy planning.

title: Improving day-ahead probabilistic solar irradiance forecasting via shape-prior flow matching for numerical weather prediction downscaling
abstract: Accurate day-ahead solar irradiance forecasting is essential for photovoltaic integration, reserve scheduling, and energy storage operation. However, operational Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) products are commonly available at hourly resolution, which limits their ability to represent sub-hourly irradiance ramps and cloud-induced fluctuations relevant to power system operation. To address this limitation, this study proposes Shape-Prior conditional Flow Matching (SPFlow), a probabilistic temporal-downscaling framework that converts hourly NWP forecasts into 15-min irradiance trajectories. SPFlow first employs a deterministic SPTransformer to construct a physically informed high-resolution shape prior from coarse NWP forecasts, satellite-derived meteorological variables, clear-sky irradiance, and site information. Conditioned on this informative prior, a conditional flow-matching model probabilistically refines the deterministic trajectory to represent unresolved sub-hourly variability and forecast uncertainty. Experiments on the SURFRAD dataset show that SPFlow consistently outperforms statistical, deterministic deep-learning, and probabilistic generative baselines. It reduces the continuous ranked probability score by up to 10.9% relative to the strongest probabilistic baseline, improves sub-hourly ramp representation, produces prediction intervals with near-nominal empirical coverage, and demonstrates promising zero-shot transferability to unseen locations. These results indicate that combining physically informed shape-prior construction with conditional flow-based probabilistic refinement provides an effective approach for converting coarse NWP forecasts into operationally useful sub-hourly probabilistic solar forecasts.

title: Trust-Aware Adaptive Disclosure for Inference Privacy Preservation in Multi-Agent Networks
abstract: Agent based systems are increasingly deployed in information critical systems including healthcare management systems, and smart grids. In this paper, we consider a multi-agent system where each agent has a latent goal that needs to be kept hidden from observing adversaries. More specifically, this paper studies privacy-preserving consensus in networked multi-agent systems under goal inference attacks. We propose a Trust-Aware Privacy Control framework that adapts message disclosure based on the dynamic trust relationships between agents. The proposed method controls information release using a trust-dependent stochastic policy. This enables a tradeoff between consensus performance and privacy preservation. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method reduces adversarial goal inference accuracy compared to representative baselines, while maintaining competitive consensus utility, thereby highlighting the effectiveness of trust-aware mechanisms in privacy preservation of the agents in multi-agent systems.
